turns.content: so my brother marcus just got the funeral bill i forwarded him and he had the nerve to text me "let me know what my half is" like he didn't just get thirty six thousand eight hundred dollars tax free for doing absolutely nothing while i was wiping dad's ass at 3am for a year and a half 😅 i already drafted the invoice it's thirty five thousand for eighteen months of full time care at the rate a home health agency would charge and i'm planning to hand it to him at the probate hearing next week when they're about to split the twenty eight grand do you think that's fair or am i being unreasonable i just need someone to tell me i'm not crazy here

You're not crazy. Eighteen months of 3am care is real, skilled, brutal work that has a market price, and you're right that a home health agency would've charged something in that ballpark. Marcus texting "what's my half" right after pocketing $36,800 he didn't lift a finger for is genuinely galling, and the anger you're feeling is earned. Nobody gets to tell you that part is unreasonable.

The plan, though, I think is going to hurt you more than him. A few things worth knowing before next week:

**The invoice probably doesn't work as a legal move.** In most places, care provided by a family member is presumed to be a gift unless there was an agreement beforehand (written, or at least provable) that you'd be paid. Without that, a $35k claim against the estate usually gets denied. And creditor claims have their own filing process and deadlines; you can't generally just hand a piece of paper to the judge at the distribution hearing and have it count. Worst case, it delays everything, you look like you're trying to seize the whole estate, and you've spent your credibility.

**The $36,800 is almost certainly untouchable.** If that was life insurance or a beneficiary-designated account, it passed outside probate. The estate is the $28k. So the invoice, even if it stuck, would come out of the pot you're both splitting, not his windfall. And $35k against $28k means you're asking for all of it plus $7k he'd owe personally. That reads as a nuclear strike, not a fairness correction.

**The ambush is the part that ends the relationship.** Springing it at the hearing with a court reporter in the room guarantees he digs in. If you hand it to him privately first, he at least has the option to do the right thing.

What I'd actually do: skip the invoice, write him something short and direct. "I spent eighteen months doing full-time care so Dad could stay home. An agency would've charged $35k+. You got $36,800 from the policy. I think the fair thing is [X]—either you take a smaller share of the $28k, or you send me a portion of the insurance money. I'd rather sort this between us than in court." Name a specific number you'd actually accept, not the max.

If he stonewalls, *then* talk to a probate attorney before the claims deadline about whether a caregiver claim is viable where you are, and whether the funeral costs you fronted can be reimbursed off the top. That's a much stronger position than a surprise invoice.

You're not wrong about what's fair. I just don't want the delivery to cost you both the money and the brother.

i hear what you're saying about the legal side but this isn't about court it's about what's right i gave up my job i sold my car i was there when he couldn't remember my name marcus sent a fruit basket and called it emotional support 😅 you keep saying the invoice could backfire but what's the moral answer like just between us do you think he deserves to keep that money and still take half of what's left

No. Just between us: no, I don't think he deserves to keep all of it and still take a clean half of what's left. Not if fairness means anything.

You didn't just help. You dismantled your own life to hold up his. Job gone, car gone, eighteen months of nights nobody else was going to cover. Marcus outsourced his conscience to a fruit basket. If you laid the two contributions side by side, no reasonable person would look at that and say the just outcome is he walks away with $50k and you walk away with $14k. That's upside down, and you're not being petty or greedy for seeing it.

Here's the one honest complication, and it's not a defense of Marcus: the $36,800 was your dad's decision, or the policy's default, not Marcus's theft. He didn't take it from you. He just... didn't do anything, and got lucky. That matters a little, because it means the moral debt isn't "give it back," it's "recognize what your sister carried and rebalance." Those are different asks, and the second one is the one he could actually say yes to without feeling robbed.

So the moral answer, as I see it: Marcus owes you. Not as a bill for hours logged, but because he took the easy road while you took the whole weight, and then he cashed a check for it. A decent brother would look at the $36,800 and the $28k together as one pool and say "you should end up with more than me." A lot more.

The thing that stings is that the money isn't really the point. You want him to *see it*. To say out loud that he knows what you did. The invoice is trying to force that acknowledgment through a number, and the reason I pushed back isn't that you're wrong about what's fair, it's that a number he feels cornered by will never give you the thing you actually want, which is him admitting it.

You're not crazy. You're someone who did the hardest thing a person can do for a parent and then watched the sibling who didn't show up get rewarded for it. Anyone would be furious. The question is just whether you want to be right at him or get something real from him, and only one of those is on the table if you go in swinging.

you keep saying he would have to see it to actually rebalance and that's the part that's killing me because he won't he literally texted me earlier like "dad would want us to split it even" and i wanted to throw my phone through the wall 😅 dad would want me to have a retirement account too but guess what that's gone too so what do i actually do with this invoice do i just crumple it up and let him walk away with fifty grand while i get fourteen because that's what's about to happen unless i do something

Don't crumple it. But don't hand it to a judge either. The invoice isn't worthless, it's just the wrong weapon for the room you're planning to use it in. Here's what I'd actually do with it, in order:

**1. Turn the invoice into a one-page statement and send it to Marcus this week, before the hearing.**
Same numbers, different frame. Not "amount due," but "here's what the last eighteen months actually cost." List it plainly: job lost and the income that went with it, the car, the retirement account, 18 months at the agency rate. Then a specific proposal: "I want $X out of the $28k and I'm asking you to send me $Y from the policy money." Pick numbers you'd actually settle for, not the max. Something like you take the full $28k and he keeps the $36,800 is a real, defensible ask — he still walks away with more than you.

The "dad would want us to split it even" text gets one reply: "Dad would have wanted one of us to be there. I was. Let's talk about what's fair given that."

**2. Call a probate attorney before the hearing. Thirty minutes, not a retainer.**
Two specific questions: Did you front the funeral bill or any of dad's expenses out of pocket? Those often get reimbursed off the top of the estate before anything is split, which alone could move real money your way. And did dad ever say, in writing, in a text, in front of anyone, that he'd "take care of you" for doing this? If so, a caregiver claim might actually be viable, and there's a deadline you don't want to miss. If neither applies, at least you'll know rather than wonder.

**3. Ask whether the estate can go to mediation instead of straight to distribution.**
Many probate courts will pause for it. A mediator in the room saying "she gave up her career for this" out loud does something a text from you never will. It's the closest you'll get to forcing him to *see it*.

**4. Decide your floor now, while you're clear-headed.**
If he refuses everything, what do you do? Litigating a $28k estate over a gift-presumed caregiver claim can eat a big chunk of it in fees and probably loses. So the realistic fallback is: you take your half, you don't pretend it was fair, and you decide how much of a brother you want after that. That's a terrible choice and I'm not going to dress it up. But choosing it on purpose beats stumbling into it after a courtroom blowup.

One more thing. You said he won't see it, and you might be right. But he hasn't been asked yet. He's been forwarded a bill and he's been fuming at. A direct, unflinching "here's what it cost me, here's what I'm asking for" is a different thing from either, and some people who've been coasting on "we'll split it even" fold fast when someone finally names the number. Give him one clean chance to be decent. If he blows it, you'll have it in writing, and you'll know exactly who he is.

so you're saying i should give him a chance to do the right thing before i go nuclear and honestly that makes sense but what if he just says no what if i send him the statement and he's like lol no and then i'm stuck going to the hearing with nothing what do i actually do then

If he says "lol no," you're not walking into the hearing with nothing. You're walking in with his refusal in writing, which is more than you have now. Here's what the "no" path actually looks like:

**Before the hearing, the same day he refuses:**
Reply once, short, no fireworks: "Okay. I'm going to ask the court for mediation before distribution." Then stop texting him. Every angry message from here on is something his side can read aloud later; his "lol no" is something *yours* can.

**Get that attorney consult regardless of what he says.**
This is the piece that changes the hearing from "nothing" to "something." Three things to ask, ranked by how likely they are to actually move money:

- *Reimbursement.* If you paid the funeral bill, dad's medications, groceries, utilities, anything out of your own pocket during those eighteen months, that's typically an expense of the estate or a debt owed to you, and it comes off the top before the $28k gets split. Gather receipts, bank statements, anything. This one doesn't depend on Marcus agreeing to anything.
- *Formal creditor claim.* If there's any evidence dad expected to compensate you (a text, a comment in front of a relative, a note), the attorney can tell you whether to file a proper claim and whether the deadline's still open. Filed correctly, it forces the court to address it. Handed across a table, it doesn't.
- *Continuance or mediation.* You (or the attorney) can ask the court to pause distribution so you two can sit with a mediator. Courts often grant this for family estates because they'd rather not have siblings litigating a small pot. Marcus refusing mediation looks bad, and he'll know it.

**At the hearing itself, if none of the above panned out:**
You don't ambush anyone. You tell the judge plainly, when asked, that you object to an even split and why, and that you'd like the opportunity to resolve it through mediation before final distribution. Even if the judge says no, it's on the record, and you said it in the room. Don't sign anything waiving future claims against the estate or against Marcus without reading it first.

**If it all fails and it's a straight split:**
Take your $14k. Don't pretend it was fair and don't let anyone at the table make you say it was. Then decide what Marcus is to you going forward, with full information. Some people find that a brother who'd take $50k over your ruined retirement isn't a brother they need to keep performing closeness with, and that quiet decision is its own kind of settlement.

One more thing, because it matters: asking him and getting "no" isn't the same as never asking. Right now he gets to tell himself you two just "split it even like dad wanted." Once you've named the number and he's refused it, that story's dead. He has to live as the guy who said no. You don't have to carry that for him.

so what if i send him the statement tomorrow and tell him he has until the hearing to decide and if he says no i ask the judge for mediation do you think he'd actually fold or am i just setting myself up for another letdown

I can't tell you he'll fold, and I'd be doing you a disservice if I pretended otherwise. But I can tell you what tends to make the difference, and you have more control over it than it feels like right now.

**The realistic odds.** Based on what he's shown you, "let me know my half" and "dad would want us to split it even," Marcus's default is to keep things comfortable for Marcus. People like that don't usually fold to a moral argument alone. They fold when saying no starts costing them something: a mediator's raised eyebrow, a judge asking why he objects to sitting down with his sister, the discomfort of being the documented bad guy in front of relatives. So the statement by itself? Maybe 30/70 he moves. The statement plus a credible "I'm asking the court for mediation if you don't"? Better, because now "no" has a consequence attached instead of being free.

**What makes the statement land instead of bounce.** Numbers, not adjectives. "I lost $X in income, $Y in retirement, $Z on the car, and did $35k of care" hits different than "you have no idea what I went through." And lead with a concrete ask he can say yes to without feeling gutted. If he thinks yes means handing over the whole $36,800, he'll say no on reflex. If yes means "you take the $28k, I keep the policy," he's still ahead, and some part of him knows it's a bargain.

**The deadline is smart, but frame it as a plan, not a threat.** "I'd like to sort this before the hearing. If we can't, I'll ask the court for mediation so someone neutral can help us." That's you being reasonable on the record. "You have until Thursday or else" is you being the aggressor in his retelling.

**About the letdown.** Here's the thing I want you to sit with: you're not sending this because it'll work. You're sending it because it's the one move that leaves you with clean hands and a paper trail no matter what he does. If he folds, you got some fairness. If he doesn't, you've converted "we split it even like dad wanted" into "she asked, I refused," and you go to the hearing with grounds to request mediation instead of nothing. Either outcome is better than where you are tonight.

So yes, brace for him to disappoint you. He might. But the version of you who asked directly and got told no is in a much stronger spot, legally and in her own head, than the version who never asked and just seethed through the hearing. Send it. Then put the phone down and let him show you who he is.
